docs.title: HitStor
docs.text: Encrypted, deduplicated backup tool written in Go.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: HitStor provides secure, efficient backups with client-side encryption, content-defined deduplication, and compression. It supports local and S3-compatible storage backends, remote backup agents over gRPC/TLS, a web dashboard, and an extensible plugin architecture.

docs.title: Key Features
docs.text:
• Client-side encryption — AES-256-GCM with scrypt key derivation
  • Content-defined deduplication — FastCDC chunking (256 KiB–4 MiB)
  • Compression — Zstd compression per chunk before encryption
  • Remote backup server — gRPC server with TLS and API key authentication
  • Web dashboard — Backup jobs, agents, storage, restore, DR workflows
  • Bare-metal restore — ReaR-based recovery media for Linux hosts
  • Plugin architecture — Storage, notifiers, hooks, filesystem scanners (go-plugin gRPC)
  • Parallel I/O — Worker pools for faster backup and restore
  • Single static binary — Zero-dependency deployment with CGO_ENABLED=0

docs.title: Quick Start
docs.text:
# Install (Linux deb)
sudo dpkg -i hitstor_0.1.0_amd64.deb

# Initialize a repository
hitstor init --repo /var/lib/hitstor/repo --password "secret"

# Create a backup
hitstor backup --repo /var/lib/hitstor/repo --password "secret" /data

# List snapshots
hitstor snapshots --repo /var/lib/hitstor/repo --password "secret"

# Restore
hitstor restore --repo /var/lib/hitstor/repo --password "secret" latest /restore

docs.title: Administration Guide
docs.text:
The HitStor Administration Guide is for system administrators responsible for deploying, configuring, and maintaining HitStor backup infrastructure. It covers server setup, agent management, TLS configuration, monitoring, and security hardening.

If you are looking for instructions on creating and restoring backups, see the User Guide instead.

docs.title: Topics
docs.text: Guide Description Server Setup Initialize a repository, start the server, configure systemd, and manage firewall rules. TLS Certificates Configure auto-generated or custom TLS certificates for gRPC and dashboard communication. Backup Jobs Filesystem backup jobs, scheduling, and retention. Agent Management Register, configure, and remove backup agents. Agent Discovery Network scan for unregistered agents. Agent Deployment Install and configure the hitstor-agent binary on Linux and Windows machines. Dashboard Access the web dashboard, manage schedules, and use the JSON API. Server Settings Central settings hub: TLS, network, integrations (Gemini), notifications. Monitoring Prometheus metrics, webhook alerting, and Grafana integration. Scheduling Configure server-managed schedules, daemon mode, and systemd timers. Sentinel Ransomware telemetry and alerts. Security Encryption model, key derivation, API key management, and systemd hardening. Troubleshooting Common errors, diagnostic commands, and log analysis. Roadmap Current priorities and out-of-scope surfaces.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: Before following the guides in this section, make sure you have HitStor installed. See the Installation Guide for platform-specific instructions.

docs.title: Conventions
docs.text:
Throughout the Administration Guide the following conventions are used:

  • Commands prefixed with $ are run in a terminal.
  • Text in UPPER_CASE (such as AGENT_NAME) represents a value you must replace with your own.
  • Optional flags are shown in square brackets: [--flag VALUE].
  • Long commands are split across multiple lines with \ for readability.
  • Configuration file paths assume a standard Linux installation. Adjust paths for other platforms as needed.

docs.title: Agent Deployment
docs.text: This guide covers installing and configuring the hitstor-agent binary on Linux and Windows machines.

docs.title: Install with the .run Installer (Recommended)
docs.text:
The .run installer includes an interactive wizard that configures the agent and starts the service automatically:

sudo ./hitstor-agent-X.Y.Z-linux-amd64.run

The wizard offers two setup modes:

docs.title: Dashboard-Managed (Recommended)
docs.text:
The agent generates a token and listens for registration from the server dashboard. No server address or API key is needed at install time.

The wizard prompts for:

  1. Setup mode — select 1 for dashboard-managed
  2. Listen port — gRPC port for server connections (default: 8422)
  3. Backup paths — optional, can be configured later from the dashboard

After installation, the wizard displays the agent token and instructions for adding the agent from the dashboard.

docs.title: Legacy (Manual)
docs.text:
The agent is configured with a server address and API key at install time. Use this if you registered the agent via hitstor serve agent add.

The wizard prompts for:

  1. Setup mode — select 2 for legacy
  2. Server address — host:port of the HitStor server
  3. API key — 64-character hex key from hitstor serve agent add <name> (masked input)
  4. Connection test — verifies connectivity before proceeding
  5. Backup paths — comma-separated directories to back up (default: /etc,/home)

docs.title: Non-Interactive Install
docs.text:
For automation, use --no-wizard with environment variables.

Dashboard-managed mode (default when no server/key env vars are set):

sudo HITSTOR_AGENT_LISTEN_PORT=8422 \
     ./hitstor-agent-X.Y.Z-linux-amd64.run --no-wizard

Legacy mode (triggered by setting server and API key):

sudo HITSTOR_AGENT_SERVER=backup.example.com:8420 \
     HITSTOR_AGENT_API_KEY=<64-char-hex-key> \
     HITSTOR_AGENT_PATHS=/etc,/home \
     ./hitstor-agent-X.Y.Z-linux-amd64.run --no-wizard

See Linux Quick Install for full details.

docs.title: Install from Package
docs.text:
Alternatively, install the agent from a deb or rpm package:

# Debian / Ubuntu
sudo apt install ./hitstor-agent_1.0.0_amd64.deb

# RHEL / Fedora / AlmaLinux
sudo rpm -i hitstor-agent-1.0.0.x86_64.rpm

See Installation for additional installation methods.

docs.title: Configure the Agent
docs.text: Configuration depends on the setup mode.

docs.title: Dashboard-Managed Agent
docs.text:
The agent reads its listen port from /etc/hitstor/agent.env:

# /etc/hitstor/agent.env
HITSTOR_AGENT_LISTEN_PORT=8422

After the server registers the agent via the dashboard, it writes the server address and API key to this file automatically. The agent token is stored at /etc/hitstor/agent-token.

To view the agent token:

sudo hitstor-agent show-id

docs.title: Legacy Agent
docs.text:
The agent reads its server address and API key from /etc/hitstor/agent.env:

# /etc/hitstor/agent.env
HITSTOR_AGENT_SERVER=backup.example.com:8420
HITSTOR_AGENT_API_KEY=a3f8c1d9e4b7...6f2a0e5d

Set file permissions so only root can read the key:

sudo chmod 0600 /etc/hitstor/agent.env
sudo chown root:root /etc/hitstor/agent.env

docs.title: Environment Variables
docs.text: Variable Description HITSTOR_AGENT_LISTEN_PORT gRPC listen port for dashboard management (default: 8422) HITSTOR_AGENT_SERVER Server address in host:port format (legacy mode) HITSTOR_AGENT_API_KEY 64-character hex API key (legacy mode) HITSTOR_AGENT_CA_CERT Path to CA certificate for TLS verification

docs.title: Retrieve the Agent Token
docs.text:
Dashboard-managed agents generate a token during installation. To display it:

sudo hitstor-agent show-id

The token is stored at /etc/hitstor/agent-token with mode 0600.

docs.title: Test the Connection (Legacy Mode)
docs.text:
For legacy agents, verify the agent can reach the server:

hitstor-agent ping

Expected output:

Server: backup.example.com:8420
Status: connected
Agent:  web-server-01

If this fails, see Troubleshooting for common connection issues.

docs.title: Run a Manual Backup
docs.text:
Create a backup of one or more directories:

hitstor-agent backup /etc /home /var/lib

The agent sends the data to the server over gRPC. Progress is displayed in the terminal.

docs.title: Daemon Mode
docs.text:
In daemon mode, the agent runs continuously with two functions:

  1. Management server — listens on port 8422 for gRPC commands from the HitStor server (registration, filesystem browsing, configuration)
  2. Backup polling — polls the server for its backup schedule and executes backups automatically
hitstor-agent daemon

If the agent is not yet registered (dashboard-managed mode), the daemon waits for registration from the dashboard and begins backing up once registered.

docs.title: Systemd Integration
docs.text: The agent package includes two systemd units:

docs.title: Daemon Mode (Recommended)
docs.text:
Enable the persistent daemon service:

sudo systemctl enable hitstor-agent
sudo systemctl start hitstor-agent

This starts hitstor-agent daemon as a long-running service. The agent listens for management commands and polls the server for schedule updates.

docs.title: Timer Mode
docs.text:
For cron-style execution, use the systemd timer instead:

sudo systemctl enable hitstor-agent.timer
sudo systemctl start hitstor-agent.timer

The timer triggers hitstor-agent backup at the configured interval. Edit the timer to customize the schedule:

sudo systemctl edit hitstor-agent.timer

[Timer]
OnCalendar=*-*-* 02:00:00

See Scheduling for more details on timer configuration.

docs.title: Check Agent Status
docs.text:
sudo systemctl status hitstor-agent
sudo journalctl -u hitstor-agent -f

docs.title: Install the Agent
docs.text: Download the Windows installer from the HitStor releases page and run it. The installer places the hitstor-agent.exe binary in C:\Program Files\HitStor\ and adds it to the system PATH.

docs.title: Configure the Agent
docs.text:
Create or edit the configuration file at C:\ProgramData\HitStor\config.yaml:

# C:\ProgramData\HitStor\config.yaml
agent_server: "backup.example.com:8420"
agent_api_key: "a3f8c1d9e4b7...6f2a0e5d"

# Optional: CA certificate for TLS verification
# agent_ca_cert: "C:\\ProgramData\\HitStor\\ca.crt"

docs.title: Test the Connection
docs.text:
Open a Command Prompt or PowerShell window:

hitstor-agent ping

docs.title: Run a Manual Backup
docs.text: hitstor-agent backup C:\Users C:\Data

docs.title: Register as a Windows Service
docs.text:
To run the agent as a background Windows Service:

hitstor-agent service install
hitstor-agent service start

This registers hitstor-agent daemon as a Windows Service that starts automatically on boot.

Manage the service:

hitstor-agent service stop
hitstor-agent service uninstall

You can also manage the service through the Windows Services console (services.msc).

docs.title: Deploying to Multiple Machines
docs.text:
For large-scale deployments, use configuration management tools (Ansible, Puppet, Chef, or similar) to:

  1. Install the hitstor-agent package
  2. The agent automatically generates a token on first start
  3. Collect agent tokens (via hitstor-agent show-id) and add agents from the dashboard
  4. Configure backup paths from the dashboard's filesystem browser

Alternatively, for legacy deployments:

  1. Register each agent with hitstor serve agent add on the server
  2. Deploy /etc/hitstor/agent.env with the machine-specific API key
  3. Deploy the CA certificate file if using self-signed certificates
  4. Enable and start the hitstor-agent systemd service

docs.text:

  • Scheduling — configure backup schedules for deployed agents
  • Monitoring — set up alerts for agent health
  • Troubleshooting — resolve connection and backup issues

docs.title: Agent Auto-Discovery
docs.text: The dashboard can discover hitstor-agent instances on your local network without manually entering every hostname.

docs.title: Workflow
docs.text:
1. Open Agents in the dashboard
  2. Click Network Discovery
  3. Select a subnet (from /api/discover/subnets) or enter a CIDR
  4. Run Scan — the server probes common agent ports
  5. Review discovered hosts and Add them with one click

docs.title: Manual Entry
docs.text:
Use Manual Entry when discovery is not possible (NAT, remote sites, non-standard ports). Provide:

  • Name — display name for the agent
  • Agent address — host:port (default agent management port: 8422)

docs.title: API
docs.text: Method Path Description GET /api/discover/subnets List local subnets POST /api/discover/scan Scan a subnet POST /api/discover/probe Probe a specific address

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Agents must run in daemon mode with AgentService listening (default port 8422)
  • Server must reach agent addresses on the network (firewall rules)
  • After discovery, complete registration by assigning an API key and backup paths

docs.title: See Also
docs.text:
• Agent Management
  • Agent Deployment

docs.title: Agent Management
docs.text: HitStor supports two methods for registering backup agents: dashboard-managed (recommended) and CLI-based (legacy). Dashboard-managed agents use a token-based flow where the server connects to the agent, authenticates, and auto-configures it. CLI-based agents use a manually-distributed API key.

docs.title: Dashboard-Managed Agents (Recommended)
docs.text: Dashboard-managed agents are added directly from the web dashboard. The server connects to the agent over gRPC, authenticates using the agent's token, and sends it the API key and server address automatically.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
1. Install the agent on the remote machine (see Agent Deployment)
  2. The agent generates a token during installation — note the token and the machine's IP address
  3. Ensure port 8422 (agent gRPC listen port) is reachable from the server

docs.title: Add an Agent from the Dashboard
docs.text:
1. Open the HitStor dashboard at http://SERVER_IP:8421
  2. Navigate to Agents
  3. Choose Network Discovery to scan local subnets, or Manual Entry to add by address
  4. For manual entry, fill in:
    • Name — descriptive identifier (for example, web-server-01)
    • Agent address — host:port (for example, 192.168.1.50:8422)
    • Token — 64-character hex token from the agent (hitstor-agent show-id on the agent machine)
  5. Click Add Agent

See Agent Discovery for the network scan workflow.

The server connects to the agent, verifies the token, sends an API key and server address, and the agent begins backing up automatically. No manual key copy is needed.

docs.title: Browse Agent Filesystem
docs.text:
For dashboard-managed agents, the Agent Detail page includes a Backup Paths section with a filesystem tree browser:

  1. Click the agent name in the Agents list
  2. Expand directories in the tree by clicking the arrow icons
  3. Check the directories you want to back up
  4. Click Save Backup Paths

The server connects to the agent over gRPC to browse its filesystem in real time. Only directories are selectable as backup paths.

docs.title: Remove an Agent
docs.text:
From the Agents list, or via the CLI:

hitstor serve agent remove AGENT_NAME

This revokes the agent's API key. The agent can no longer connect to the server. Existing snapshots created by the agent are not deleted.

docs.title: CLI-Based Agents (Legacy)
docs.text: CLI-based agents are registered from the server command line. The API key must be manually copied to the agent machine.

docs.title: Register an Agent
docs.text:
hitstor serve agent add AGENT_NAME

On success, the command prints a 64-character hexadecimal API key:

Agent "web-server-01" registered.
API Key: a3f8c1d9e4b7...6f2a0e5d (64 characters)

Store this key securely. It cannot be displayed again.

Copy this key to the agent's /etc/hitstor/agent.env file.

docs.title: List Agents
docs.text:
View all registered agents (both managed and CLI-based):

hitstor serve agent list

Output:

NAME              STATUS     LAST BACKUP           SNAPSHOTS
web-server-01     active     2026-02-21 03:00:12   47
db-primary        active     2026-02-21 03:15:08   47
staging-app       stale      2026-02-19 12:30:00   23

docs.title: Remove an Agent
docs.text:
hitstor serve agent remove AGENT_NAME

To remove an agent and all of its snapshots:

hitstor serve agent remove AGENT_NAME --purge-snapshots

docs.title: Agent Status
docs.text:
The status column shows:

Status Meaning active Agent has backed up within the stale threshold stale Agent has not backed up within the stale threshold (default: 25 hours) new Agent is registered but has never completed a backup

docs.title: Agent Token (Dashboard-Managed)
docs.text:
Dashboard-managed agents authenticate using a token — a 64-character hexadecimal string (256 bits of entropy) generated during agent installation.

Token properties:

  • Generated automatically during install, stored at /etc/hitstor/agent-token (mode 0600)
  • Retrievable any time with sudo hitstor-agent show-id
  • Stored encrypted (AES-256-GCM) on the server in the agent registry
  • Used by the server to authenticate gRPC calls to the agent (browse filesystem, configure paths)

docs.title: API Key Security (CLI-Based)
docs.text:
CLI-based agents authenticate to the server using a 64-character hexadecimal API key (256 bits of entropy).

Key properties:

  • One key per agent
  • Displayed only once at registration time
  • Cannot be retrieved or displayed again after registration
  • Stored encrypted in the agent registry alongside the repository

Best practices:

  • Copy the key directly into the agent's environment file at registration time
  • Do not store keys in version control, wikis, or chat logs
  • If a key is compromised, remove the agent and re-register it

docs.title: Rotating an API Key
docs.text:
1. Remove the agent: hitstor serve agent remove AGENT_NAME
  2. Re-register the agent: hitstor serve agent add AGENT_NAME
  3. Update the agent's configuration with the new key
  4. Restart the agent service

Existing snapshots are preserved as long as --purge-snapshots is not used.

docs.title: Agent Registry
docs.text:
The agent registry is an encrypted data structure stored alongside the repository. It contains:

  • Agent names and hashed API keys
  • Agent metadata (registration time, last backup time, snapshot count)
  • Per-agent scheduling configuration
  • For managed agents: encrypted token and agent address

The registry is encrypted with the repository key and cannot be read without the repository password.

docs.title: Next Steps
docs.text:
• Agent Deployment — install and configure agents on remote machines
  • Dashboard — view and manage agents from the web interface
  • Monitoring — set up alerts for stale agents

docs.title: Backup Jobs
docs.text: The dashboard Backups page (/backups) is the central place to define what gets backed up and when. Each backup job has a job_type that determines how data is collected.

docs.title: Job Types
docs.text:
Type Collector Runs on files Agent filesystem scan via built-in plugin (hitstor-scanner-builtin, shipped with agent) or custom scanner plugin Remote agent

files is the only supported job type. SaaS, database, and cloud-VM job types were permanently removed in v2.0.0 — see the Roadmap. Legacy jobs of those types are loaded but disabled on startup.

docs.title: Filesystem Jobs
docs.text:
The default job type. The server assigns paths and schedule to an agent; the agent scans, chunks, and uploads new data.

  • Configure paths via the job detail page or agent browse UI
  • Enable VSS on Windows agents for consistent snapshots
  • Set full rescan interval (days) to guard against silent corruption
  • Use Force full backup from the dashboard when needed

docs.title: Scheduling
docs.text:
Each job supports:

  • Interval — every N hours
  • Cron — 5-field cron with IANA timezone
  • Visual schedule builder — daily / weekly / monthly presets

The agent daemon polls GetSchedule every 5 minutes (default). "Backup Now" sends a WakeUp RPC for immediate pickup.

docs.title: Cancel Running Backups
docs.text: POST /api/backups/{id}/cancel aborts an active session. Stale sessions (no activity for 10+ minutes) show a warning badge on the dashboard.

docs.title: API
docs.text: See Dashboard HTTP API — Backup Jobs.

docs.title: Web Dashboard
docs.text: HitStor includes a built-in web dashboard for monitoring backup infrastructure, managing agents, browsing remote filesystems, and configuring schedules. The dashboard is served by the same hitstor serve process that handles gRPC connections.

docs.title: Accessing the Dashboard
docs.text:
The dashboard is available at:

http://SERVER_IP:8421

Replace SERVER_IP with the hostname or IP address of the HitStor server. The default dashboard port is 8421, configurable with --dashboard-port.

docs.title: Password Protection
docs.text:
The dashboard always requires a password. Set it with the serve_dashboard_password configuration key:

# /etc/hitstor/config.yaml
serve_dashboard_password: "DASHBOARD_PASSWORD"

If no password is configured, hitstor serve generates a random one at startup, stores its hash in the config file and prints the plaintext once in the server log (look for no dashboard password configured). Log in with it and change it under Settings. If the server has no config file, a new password is generated on every restart.

The dashboard presents a login page. Authentication uses session cookies with the following security properties:

  • HttpOnly — cookies are not accessible to JavaScript
  • SameSite=Strict — cookies are not sent on cross-site requests

Sessions expire when the browser is closed.

docs.title: Update Notifications
docs.text:
When update_check: true is set in the configuration (the default), the server checks for new releases via the GitHub Releases API every 24 hours. If a newer version is available, a notification banner appears at the top of every dashboard page:

HitStor v1.1.0 is available (current: v1.0.0). View release

The banner links to the release page on GitHub. To disable automatic checks, set update_check: false in /etc/hitstor/config.yaml. You can also check manually from the CLI with hitstor version --check.

docs.title: Layout
docs.text:
The dashboard uses a fixed header bar with the HitStor logo and version, a sidebar with icon navigation, and a main content area. The sidebar groups pages into two sections:

  • Monitoring — Overview, Backups, Agents
  • Management — Storage, Settings

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The main page displays a summary of the backup infrastructure:

  • Total number of agents, snapshots, and last backup time
  • Agent health breakdown (OK, stale, never backed up)
  • Quick links to Agents, Snapshots, and Storage pages

docs.title: Agents
docs.text:
Lists all registered agents with their current status, type (managed or CLI), last backup time, and creation date. Click an agent name to view its detail page.

Adding an agent from the dashboard:

  1. Use Network Discovery to scan subnets, or Manual Entry for a specific host:port
  2. Enter the agent name, agent_addr, and token (manual entry)
  3. Confirm registration

The server connects to the agent over AgentService (port 8422), verifies the token, and sends API key + server address. See Agent Management and Agent Discovery.

docs.title: Agent Detail
docs.text:
Shows detailed information for a single agent:

  • Target Repository — select which repository this agent backs up to
  • Backup Schedule — enable/disable scheduled backups, set interval in hours
  • Backup Paths (managed agents only) — filesystem tree browser for selecting directories to back up
  • Snapshot History — table with snapshot IDs, timestamps, file counts, sizes, and durations

docs.title: Filesystem Tree Browser
docs.text:
For dashboard-managed agents, the Backup Paths section displays a live filesystem tree from the agent machine. The server connects to the agent over gRPC to list directories in real time.

  • Click the arrow icon to expand a directory and load its contents
  • Check the directories you want to include in backups
  • Click Save Backup Paths to send the configuration to the agent

Directories that are not readable by the agent process appear dimmed.

docs.title: Snapshots
docs.text: Lists all snapshots across all agents. Supports filtering by agent name. Each entry shows the snapshot ID, agent, timestamp, paths, file count, and total size.

docs.title: Storage
docs.text:
The Storage page provides full repository management:

  • Repository list — view all configured repositories (local and S3) with status badges, disk usage bars, snapshot counts, and pack/index statistics
  • Create repository — initialize a new local or S3-compatible repository directly from the dashboard. Local repositories show available disk space and detect existing repos at the given path
  • Connect existing repository — if a repository already exists at a path (for example, after reinstalling), the dashboard detects it and connects instead of reinitializing
  • Disconnect repository — remove a repository from the configuration (does not delete data on disk)
  • Integrity check — run hitstor check on a repository with real-time progress via Server-Sent Events. Results show pass/fail status and any errors found
  • Prune — free space by removing unreferenced data, with confirmation dialog and live progress. Shows packs deleted, bytes freed, and indexes rewritten
  • Growth chart — visualize storage growth over time with configurable date range (30 days, 90 days, 6 months, 1 year, all) and granularity (daily, weekly)
  • Snapshot detail — browse snapshot contents and restore individual files or whole paths. See Restore.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text: Central hub for server configuration: general performance, TLS, network ports, Integrations (Gemini), and notifications. See Server Settings.

docs.title: Schedule Management
docs.text:
The dashboard allows administrators to configure per-agent backup schedules without logging into the server command line.

From the Agent Detail page:

  1. Toggle scheduling on or off for the agent
  2. Set the backup interval in hours (for example, every 24 hours)
  3. Click Save Schedule

Agents running in daemon mode (hitstor-agent daemon) poll the server for schedule updates and execute backups accordingly.

docs.title: JSON API
docs.text: The dashboard exposes a JSON API for programmatic access. All endpoints return JSON responses.

docs.title: Endpoints
docs.text: Method Path Description GET /api/agents List all registered agents with status POST /api/agents Add a dashboard-managed agent (name, address, token) DELETE /api/agents/{name} Remove an agent POST /api/agents/{name}/schedule Update agent backup schedule POST /api/agents/{name}/repo Set agent target repository POST /api/agents/{name}/browse Browse agent filesystem (managed agents) POST /api/agents/{name}/configure Configure agent backup paths (managed agents) GET /api/agents/{name}/info Query agent info (managed agents) GET /api/snapshots List all snapshots (supports ?agent=NAME filter) GET /api/stats Repository statistics (storage, deduplication, counts) GET /api/repos List all configured repositories POST /api/repos Create a new repository (local or S3) DELETE /api/repos/{name} Disconnect a repository POST /api/repos/test-s3 Test S3 endpoint connectivity POST /api/repos/detect Detect existing repository at a path GET /api/repos/{name}/growth Storage growth data for charting GET /api/repos/{name}/sessions Active backup sessions for a repository POST /api/repos/{name}/check Start integrity check (returns operation ID) POST /api/repos/{name}/prune Start prune operation (returns operation ID) GET /api/operations/{id}/events SSE stream for operation progress GET /api/disk-space Available disk space at a given path

docs.title: Example: Add an Agent
docs.text:
curl -X POST http://localhost:8421/api/agents \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"name":"web-01","address":"192.168.1.50:8422","token":"a3f8c1d9e4b7..."}'

docs.title: Example: Browse Agent Filesystem
docs.text:
curl -X POST http://localhost:8421/api/agents/web-01/browse \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"path":"/home"}'

docs.title: Example: List Agents
docs.text:
curl -s http://localhost:8421/api/agents | jq .

If dashboard password protection is enabled, include the session cookie or authenticate first:

# Authenticate and save cookie
curl -c cookies.txt -d "password=DASHBOARD_PASSWORD" http://localhost:8421/login

# Use cookie for API requests
curl -b cookies.txt -s http://localhost:8421/api/stats | jq .

docs.title: Prometheus Metrics
docs.text:
The dashboard exposes a Prometheus-compatible metrics endpoint:

http://SERVER_IP:8421/metrics

This endpoint is unauthenticated (accessible without the dashboard password) to allow Prometheus to scrape metrics without credential management. If this is a concern, restrict access at the network level.

See Monitoring for the full list of metrics and Prometheus configuration.

docs.title: Next Steps
docs.text:
• Agent Management — register and manage agents
  • Monitoring — configure Prometheus scraping and alerting
  • Scheduling — detailed scheduling configuration options
  • Security — dashboard authentication and hardening

docs.title: Monitoring and Alerting
docs.text: HitStor provides Prometheus metrics and webhook alerting to integrate with existing monitoring infrastructure.

docs.title: Prometheus Metrics
docs.text:
The server exposes a Prometheus-compatible metrics endpoint at:

http://SERVER_IP:8421/metrics

This endpoint is unauthenticated, allowing Prometheus to scrape without credential configuration. Restrict access at the network level if needed.

docs.title: Available Metrics
docs.text: HitStor exports 14 metrics: 9 gauges, 4 counters, and 1 per-agent metric.

docs.title: Gauges
docs.text: Metric Type Description hitstor_agents_total gauge Total number of registered agents hitstor_agents_active gauge Number of agents with recent backups hitstor_agents_stale gauge Number of agents past the stale threshold hitstor_snapshots_total gauge Total number of snapshots in the repository hitstor_storage_bytes gauge Total repository size in bytes hitstor_storage_raw_bytes gauge Total size of original (pre-dedup) data in bytes hitstor_dedup_ratio gauge Deduplication ratio (raw / stored) hitstor_packs_total gauge Number of pack files in the repository hitstor_uptime_seconds gauge Server uptime in seconds

docs.title: Counters
docs.text: Metric Type Description hitstor_backups_total counter Total number of completed backups since server start hitstor_backups_failed_total counter Total number of failed backups since server start hitstor_restores_total counter Total number of completed restores since server start hitstor_bytes_received_total counter Total bytes received from agents since server start

docs.title: Per-Agent Metric
docs.text: Metric Type Labels Description hitstor_agent_last_backup_timestamp gauge agent Unix timestamp of the agent's last successful backup

docs.title: Prometheus Scrape Configuration
docs.text:
Add the following to your prometheus.yml:

scrape_configs:
  - job_name: "hitstor"
    scrape_interval: 30s
    static_configs:
      - targets: ["backup.example.com:8421"]

For multiple HitStor servers:

scrape_configs:
  - job_name: "hitstor"
    scrape_interval: 30s
    static_configs:
      - targets:
          - "backup-01.example.com:8421"
          - "backup-02.example.com:8421"

docs.title: Grafana Dashboard
docs.text:
To build a Grafana dashboard for HitStor:

  1. Add your Prometheus instance as a data source in Grafana.
  2. Create a new dashboard with panels for key metrics:

Suggested panels:

Panel Query Visualization Active Agents hitstor_agents_active Stat Stale Agents hitstor_agents_stale Stat (red threshold > 0) Total Snapshots hitstor_snapshots_total Stat Storage Used hitstor_storage_bytes Stat (unit: bytes) Dedup Ratio hitstor_dedup_ratio Stat Backup Rate rate(hitstor_backups_total[1h]) Time series Failed Backups rate(hitstor_backups_failed_total[1h]) Time series (alert threshold) Data Ingestion rate(hitstor_bytes_received_total[5m]) Time series (unit: bytes/s) Last Backup per Agent hitstor_agent_last_backup_timestamp Table
  1. Set up Grafana alerts on hitstor_agents_stale > 0 and rate(hitstor_backups_failed_total[1h]) > 0.

docs.title: Webhook Alerting
docs.text: HitStor can send webhook notifications when backup failures or stale agents are detected.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
Set the webhook URL in the config file:

# /etc/hitstor/config.yaml
alert_webhook_url: "https://hooks.example.com/hitstor"
alert_stale_threshold: 25
Key Type Default Description alert_webhook_url string (none) URL to POST alert payloads to alert_stale_threshold integer 25 Hours without a backup before an agent is considered stale

docs.title: Alert Events
docs.text: HitStor sends alerts for two event types:

docs.title: backup_failed
docs.text:
Sent immediately when a backup fails.

{
  "event": "backup_failed",
  "agent": "web-server-01",
  "timestamp": "2026-02-21T03:05:00Z",
  "error": "connection reset by peer",
  "server": "backup.example.com"
}

docs.title: agent_stale
docs.text:
Sent when an agent has not completed a backup within the stale threshold.

{
  "event": "agent_stale",
  "agent": "staging-app",
  "timestamp": "2026-02-21T14:00:00Z",
  "last_backup": "2026-02-19T12:30:00Z",
  "threshold_hours": 25,
  "server": "backup.example.com"
}

docs.title: Cooldown and Recovery
docs.text:
To avoid alert fatigue, HitStor applies cooldown logic:

  • After sending a stale alert for an agent, it does not re-alert until the threshold duration has elapsed again.
  • When a stale agent completes a successful backup, the alert state is cleared. If the agent goes stale again, a new alert is sent.
  • Failed backup alerts have no cooldown -- each failure triggers a notification.

docs.title: Notifier Plugins
docs.text:
For custom notification delivery (Slack, PagerDuty, email, etc.), use notifier plugins instead of or in addition to the webhook.

Configure notifier plugins in the config file:

# /etc/hitstor/config.yaml
alert_notifier_plugins:
  - /usr/lib/hitstor/plugins/slack-notifier
  - /usr/lib/hitstor/plugins/pagerduty-notifier

Notifier plugins receive the same JSON payload as the webhook and can transform it for their target system. See the Plugins documentation for details on writing and installing plugins.

docs.title: Next Steps
docs.text:
• Dashboard -- view metrics and agent status in the web UI
  • Scheduling -- configure backup schedules to keep agents active
  • Troubleshooting -- diagnose stale agents and failed backups

docs.title: Roadmap
docs.text: HitStor is a filesystem backup and restore product for Windows and Linux, and the roadmap exists to make it excellent at exactly that. Work that does not improve backing up and restoring files fast, safely, and verifiably is out of scope by default.

docs.title: Shipped
docs.text: Item Notes Deduplication & encryption engine FastCDC chunking, Zstd, AES-256-GCM, scrypt KDF Server / agent architecture gRPC over TLS, thick agent chunks and compresses locally Web dashboard Jobs, agents, storage, restores, progress via SSE Incremental backups & synthetic full Parent-snapshot reuse, periodic full rescan Advanced scheduling Interval, 5-field cron, timezone-aware with DST handling Agent auto-discovery Network scan for unregistered agents Snapshot restore File-tree browse, granular and whole-path restore Restore verification Automated post-backup restore checks per job Consistent snapshots VSS (Windows), LVM and btrfs (Linux) Guided disaster recovery Multi-job full-system restore onto a rebuilt host Benchmarks Reproducible backup/restore harness, optional restic comparison Ransomware Sentinel Gemini telemetry over filesystem snapshots (optional)

docs.title: Now
docs.text: Item Goal Bare-metal restore Bootable recovery media plus the metadata needed to rebuild a bootable system — see below

docs.title: Next
docs.text: Item Goal Remote filesystem restore Restore to an agent in another network or a cloud VM Restore performance Parallel restore streams and resume after interruption

docs.title: Bare-metal restore (in design)
docs.text:
Today's disaster recovery wizard restores files onto a host that already boots and already runs a registered agent. True bare-metal restore additionally requires:

  1. Boot media — a bootable Linux/WinPE image carrying the agent, so a machine with a blank disk can be recovered.
  2. Richer file metadata — Windows security descriptors and POSIX ACLs/xattrs (including SELinux contexts), which the current snapshot format does not capture.
  3. Disk layout capture — partition table, filesystem UUIDs, and LVM configuration, so partitions can be recreated and /etc/fstab still resolves.
  4. Bootloader reconstruction — GRUB/EFI on Linux and BCD on Windows.

Restoring files alone onto a blank disk produces an unbootable system, so these land together rather than as independent features.

docs.title: Permanently removed (v2.0.0)
docs.text:
These are not deferred — they were removed from the product and are not planned to return:

  • Microsoft 365 and Google Workspace backup
  • Database backup (PostgreSQL, MySQL, MariaDB, SQL Server, Oracle)
  • Cloud VM agentless backup (GCP, AWS, Azure) and VMware/vSphere
  • The workload collector plugin type that served them

Existing config.yaml files containing collector_plugins or the related integration keys still load; those keys are simply ignored (unknown fields).

docs.title: Also not on the roadmap
docs.text: Autonomous DR (auto-failover, LLM-generated bootstrap scripts, DNS promotion, scheduled RPO/RTO drills) remains out of scope. If demand returns, it should build on agent-based restore rather than bespoke cloud provisioning.

docs.title: See also
docs.text:
• Disaster Recovery
  • Restore
  • Sentinel
  • Codebase Overview

docs.title: Backup Scheduling
docs.text: HitStor supports several approaches to scheduling automatic backups. Choose the method that best fits your infrastructure.

docs.title: Server-Managed Scheduling
docs.text: The recommended approach is server-managed scheduling, where backup schedules are configured centrally and agents poll the server for their next run time.

docs.title: Configure from the Dashboard
docs.text:
1. Open the Dashboard at http://SERVER_IP:8421.
  2. Navigate to Backups and click + New Backup Job (or open an existing job).
  3. Choose a schedule mode:
    • Interval: Run every N hours (simple, no timezone awareness).
    • Cron Expression: Use standard 5-field cron syntax for precise scheduling with timezone support.
  4. If using Cron mode, enter the expression and select a timezone. The dashboard validates the expression and shows a human-readable description with the next 3 run times.
  5. Save the configuration.

The server stores schedule configuration in the agent registry. Agents running in daemon mode pick up changes automatically.

docs.title: Interval Mode
docs.text:
The simplest scheduling option. Set the number of hours between backups:

  • How it works: next_run = last_backup + interval_hours
  • Timezone: Not applicable (relative to last backup time)
  • Best for: Simple setups where exact run times don't matter

docs.title: Cron Expression Mode
docs.text:
Standard 5-field cron syntax for precise, timezone-aware scheduling:

┌───────────── minute (0-59)
│ ┌───────────── hour (0-23)
│ │ ┌───────────── day of month (1-31)
│ │ │ ┌───────────── month (1-12)
│ │ │ │ ┌───────────── day of week (0-6, Sun=0)
│ │ │ │ │
* * * * *

Supported syntax:

Syntax Example Meaning Wildcard * Every value Specific value 5 Only at 5 List 1,15 At 1 and 15 Range 1-5 1 through 5 Step */15 Every 15 units Range with step 0-30/10 0, 10, 20, 30

Common examples:

Expression Description 0 2 * * * Daily at 2:00 AM 0 3 * * 1-5 Weekdays at 3:00 AM 30 1 * * 0 Sundays at 1:30 AM 0 */6 * * * Every 6 hours 0 22 1 * * 1st of each month at 10:00 PM */15 * * * * Every 15 minutes

Timezone handling:

  • Select a timezone from the dropdown (IANA format, e.g. America/New_York).
  • If no timezone is selected, the server's local timezone is used.
  • Cron expressions are evaluated in the selected timezone, handling DST transitions automatically:
    • Spring forward: If a scheduled time falls in the skipped hour, the backup runs at the next valid time.
    • Fall back: If a scheduled time falls in the repeated hour, the backup runs on the first occurrence.

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text:
1. The agent calls the GetSchedule RPC on the server.
  2. The server evaluates the schedule (cron expression or interval) and responds with the next run time (next_run).
  3. The agent sleeps until next_run, then executes the backup.
  4. After the backup completes, the agent calls GetSchedule again for the next run.

This approach allows administrators to change schedules from the dashboard without restarting or reconfiguring agents.

docs.title: Missed Window Recovery
docs.text:
If the server or agent is offline when a backup was due:

  • On the next poll, the server detects that now > next_run and signals the agent to run immediately.
  • After the catch-up backup, the schedule advances to the next future occurrence (no double-runs).
  • This works for both interval and cron modes.

docs.title: Agent Daemon Mode
docs.text:
Daemon mode is the client-side component of server-managed scheduling. Start the agent in daemon mode:

hitstor-agent daemon

In daemon mode, the agent:

  • Runs as a long-lived process
  • Polls the server for its backup schedule via the GetSchedule RPC (default: every 5 minutes)
  • Executes backups when now >= next_run_unix for any enabled job
  • Reports backup results back to the server
  • Handles transient connection failures with automatic retry

docs.title: Systemd Service (Linux)
docs.text:
Enable the daemon as a systemd service:

sudo systemctl enable hitstor-agent
sudo systemctl start hitstor-agent

The service unit runs hitstor-agent daemon with restart-on-failure.

docs.title: Windows Service
docs.text:
Register the daemon as a Windows Service:

hitstor-agent service install
hitstor-agent service start

The service starts automatically on boot. See Agent Deployment for full Windows setup instructions.

docs.title: Systemd Timer (Alternative)
docs.text: If you prefer cron-style scheduling managed at the OS level rather than server-managed scheduling, use a systemd timer.

docs.title: Enable the Timer
docs.text:
sudo systemctl enable hitstor-agent.timer
sudo systemctl start hitstor-agent.timer

The timer triggers the hitstor-agent service unit, which runs a single backup and exits.

docs.title: Customize the Schedule
docs.text:
Override the default timer schedule:

sudo systemctl edit hitstor-agent.timer

Add an [Timer] section with your desired OnCalendar value:

[Timer]
OnCalendar=*-*-* 02:00:00

docs.title: OnCalendar Syntax
docs.text:
The OnCalendar directive uses systemd calendar event syntax. Common examples:

Expression Schedule *-*-* 02:00:00 Daily at 2:00 AM *-*-* 00/6:00:00 Every 6 hours (midnight, 6 AM, noon, 6 PM) *-*-* *:00:00 Every hour Mon *-*-* 03:00:00 Every Monday at 3:00 AM *-*-01 04:00:00 First day of each month at 4:00 AM *-*-* 02:00:00,14:00:00 Twice daily at 2:00 AM and 2:00 PM

Verify the schedule with systemd-analyze:

systemd-analyze calendar "*-*-* 02:00:00"

docs.title: Timer vs. Daemon Mode
docs.text:
Feature Daemon Mode Timer Mode Schedule source Server (dashboard) Local systemd timer Central management Yes No (per-machine) Dynamic schedule changes Yes (via dashboard) Requires systemd edit Process lifecycle Long-running Starts per backup Server connection Persistent On-demand

Daemon mode is recommended for most deployments because it enables centralized schedule management.

docs.title: Windows Task Scheduler
docs.text:
On Windows systems where the agent is not registered as a Windows Service, use Task Scheduler as an alternative:

  1. Open Task Scheduler (taskschd.msc).
  2. Create a new basic task.
  3. Set the trigger to the desired schedule (for example, daily at 2:00 AM).
  4. Set the action to start a program:
    • Program: C:\Program Files\HitStor\hitstor-agent.exe
    • Arguments: backup C:\Users C:\Data
  5. Save the task.

For server-managed scheduling on Windows, use daemon mode via the Windows Service instead.

docs.title: Scheduling Best Practices
docs.text:
• Use cron expressions for production deployments. They provide precise, timezone-aware scheduling that handles DST transitions and server restarts correctly.
  • Stagger backup times across agents to avoid overloading the server with simultaneous backups. With cron expressions, use different minutes (e.g., 0 2 * * * for one agent, 15 2 * * * for another).
  • Use off-peak hours (for example, 01:00 to 05:00) to minimize impact on production workloads.
  • Always set a timezone when using cron expressions to avoid ambiguity across servers in different locations.
  • Set the stale threshold (alert_stale_threshold) to slightly more than the backup interval. For daily backups, 25 hours is a reasonable default.
  • Monitor scheduling via the dashboard and Prometheus metrics to ensure backups run on time.

docs.title: Next Steps
docs.text:
• Agent Deployment -- install agents and configure systemd units
  • Monitoring -- set up alerts for missed backups
  • Dashboard -- manage schedules from the web interface

docs.title: Security
docs.text: This page documents the HitStor security model, covering encryption, key management, authentication, and system hardening.

docs.title: Data Encryption
docs.text:
All data stored in the repository is encrypted with AES-256-GCM (Galois/Counter Mode). Encryption is applied client-side before data is written to storage, ensuring that the repository contents are unreadable without the password.

Each blob (chunk of data) is encrypted with a unique nonce. The authenticated encryption provided by GCM ensures both confidentiality and integrity -- any tampering with encrypted data is detected on read.

docs.title: Key Derivation
docs.text:
The encryption key is derived from the repository password using scrypt with the following parameters:

Parameter Value Purpose N 32768 CPU/memory cost factor r 8 Block size p 1 Parallelization factor

These parameters are designed to make brute-force attacks computationally expensive. The scrypt output produces two keys:

  • EncKey -- used for AES-256-GCM encryption of data blobs
  • IDKey -- used for HMAC-SHA256 blob identification

docs.title: Blob Identification
docs.text:
Blob IDs are computed as HMAC-SHA256 using the IDKey derived from the password. This prevents content-guessing attacks: an attacker who knows the plaintext content of a file cannot determine whether it exists in the repository without knowing the password.

BlobID = HMAC-SHA256(IDKey, plaintext)

Without the IDKey, an attacker cannot correlate known plaintext with stored blobs.

docs.title: TLS
docs.text:
All gRPC communication between agents and the server is encrypted with TLS. The server either auto-generates a self-signed certificate or uses custom certificates provided by the administrator.

Configuration Encryption Certificate Verification Auto-generated (default) Yes Agent must set agent_ca_cert Custom certificate Yes Standard CA verification or agent_ca_cert Let's Encrypt Yes Standard CA verification (no extra config)

TLS is always enabled. There is no option to disable transport encryption.

See TLS Certificates for detailed configuration.

docs.title: Agent Authentication
docs.text:
HitStor uses two authentication mechanisms for agents:

Agent tokens (dashboard-managed agents):

  • 64-character hexadecimal string (256 bits of entropy)
  • Generated automatically during agent installation
  • Stored at /etc/hitstor/agent-token on the agent (mode 0600)
  • Stored encrypted (AES-256-GCM) on the server in the agent registry
  • Used by the server to authenticate gRPC calls to the agent (filesystem browsing, configuration)
  • Retrievable any time with hitstor-agent show-id
  • Verified using constant-time comparison to prevent timing attacks

API keys (all agents):

  • 64-character hexadecimal string (256 bits of entropy)
  • One key per agent
  • Generated using a cryptographically secure random number generator
  • For dashboard-managed agents: sent to the agent automatically during registration
  • For CLI-registered agents: displayed once at registration time and cannot be retrieved again
  • Stored as a hash in the encrypted agent registry

An agent must present a valid API key with every backup gRPC request. The server verifies the key against the hashed value in the registry.

docs.title: Repository Password
docs.text:
The repository password is the root secret for all encryption operations. It is:

  • Never stored on disk by the server (provided at runtime via environment variable or password file)
  • Used to derive EncKey and IDKey through scrypt
  • Required to read or write any data in the repository

If the password is lost, the repository data is irrecoverable.

docs.title: Dashboard Authentication
docs.text:
The web dashboard always requires login. The password comes from serve_dashboard_password; when it is not set, the server generates a random password at startup, stores its scrypt hash in the config file and logs the plaintext once so the operator can sign in and change it.

Session cookies have the following security properties:

Property Value Purpose HttpOnly true Prevents JavaScript access to the cookie SameSite Strict Prevents cross-site request forgery (CSRF)

The /metrics endpoint is excluded from authentication to allow Prometheus scraping. Restrict access to this endpoint at the network level if needed.

docs.title: Systemd Hardening
docs.text:
The HitStor server systemd unit includes security hardening directives that restrict the server process:

[Service]
# Filesystem protection
ProtectSystem=strict
ProtectHome=true
ReadWritePaths=/var/lib/hitstor

# Privilege restrictions
NoNewPrivileges=true
PrivateTmp=true

# Capability restrictions
CapabilityBoundingSet=
AmbientCapabilities=

# Network
RestrictAddressFamilies=AF_INET AF_INET6 AF_UNIX

# System call filtering
SystemCallFilter=@system-service
SystemCallArchitectures=native

# Namespace isolation
PrivateDevices=true
ProtectKernelTunables=true
ProtectKernelModules=true
ProtectControlGroups=true

These directives:

  • Prevent the server from writing outside its data directory
  • Block privilege escalation
  • Restrict system calls to the minimum required set
  • Isolate the process from kernel tunables and device access

docs.title: Verifying Hardening
docs.text:
Check the security score of the unit:

systemd-analyze security hitstor-server

A score below 5.0 indicates good hardening. Review any items marked as "UNSAFE" and assess whether they are required for your deployment.

docs.title: Security Checklist
docs.text:
Use this checklist when deploying HitStor in production:

  • [ ] Use a strong repository password (at least 16 characters, randomly generated)
  • [ ] Store the password in a file with 0600 permissions, not on the command line
  • [ ] Use custom TLS certificates from a trusted CA
  • [ ] Set a dashboard password (serve_dashboard_password)
  • [ ] Restrict dashboard port (8421) to management networks
  • [ ] Restrict the /metrics endpoint to Prometheus scraper IPs
  • [ ] Enable systemd hardening (included by default in packaged units)
  • [ ] Ensure agent token files (/etc/hitstor/agent-token) have 0600 permissions
  • [ ] Restrict agent gRPC port (8422) to the server's IP address
  • [ ] Rotate API keys if compromise is suspected (remove and re-register the agent)
  • [ ] Run hitstor check --read-data periodically to verify repository integrity
  • [ ] Keep HitStor updated to receive security fixes

docs.title: Next Steps
docs.text:
• TLS Certificates -- configure production TLS
  • Agent Management -- API key registration and rotation
  • Troubleshooting -- diagnose security-related issues

docs.title: Ransomware Sentinel
docs.text: HitStor Sentinel (internal/sentinel) monitors backup session telemetry for ransomware-like behavior using Google Gemini. When risk is elevated, it can alert administrators and apply protective actions such as agent suspension and storage retention locks.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
After every backup session finalizes, the server:

  1. Gathers up to 10 prior snapshots for the same host as a baseline.
  2. Sends the current session's telemetry plus that baseline to Gemini for analysis.
  3. If the analysis reports a threat with confidence at or above HITSTOR_SENTINEL_THRESHOLD (default 0.8), the server:
  4. Suspends the agent's credentials, blocking further backups from that host.
  5. Locks the configured storage bucket with an immutable retention hold, so ransomware cannot delete historical snapshots even with valid credentials.
  6. Fires an alert, visible via GET /api/alerts and any configured webhook/notifier.

This only runs the containment steps above the confidence threshold — most backups complete with Sentinel silently finding nothing.

docs.title: Telemetry Signals
docs.text:
• FastCDC compression ratios (encrypted/random data compresses poorly)
  • Mass file change or deletion rates
  • Session-level anomaly patterns compared to the host's own history

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
Sentinel is enabled by default when the server starts. It is configured entirely through environment variables read at hitstor serve startup — there is no hitstor config set equivalent. The Gemini API key/model fall back to the encrypted integrations.* values in config.yaml (set via Settings → Integrations) when the Sentinel-specific variables are unset.

See Environment Variables → Sentinel for the full variable list, defaults, and the three supported retention-lock backends (GCS, S3, Azure Blob).

Configure alerting alongside existing webhook and notifier plugins:

alert_webhook_url: https://hooks.slack.com/services/...
alert_notifier_plugins:
  - slack
plugin_dir: /usr/local/lib/hitstor/plugins

docs.title: Dashboard Alerts
docs.text: Active sentinel alerts appear via GET /api/alerts. Resolve handled incidents with POST /api/alerts/{id}/resolve.

docs.title: Retention Lock
docs.text: For supported object storage backends (GCS, S3, Azure Blob), Sentinel can trigger immutable retention locks on the backup bucket to prevent ransomware from deleting historical snapshots — even with valid, unrevoked credentials. This is separate from the repository's own backend (local/S3); the lock targets whichever bucket HITSTOR_SENTINEL_BACKEND_TYPE and its bucket variable point at.

docs.title: See Also
docs.text:
• Monitoring
  • Security
  • Environment Variables

docs.title: Server Setup
docs.text: This guide covers deploying the HitStor server, including repository initialization, server startup, systemd integration, and firewall configuration.

docs.title: Create a Repository
docs.text:
Repositories can be created in two ways:

  1. From the dashboard (recommended): Navigate to Storage and click New Repository. The dashboard guides you through creating a local or S3-compatible repository.
  2. From the CLI:
hitstor init --repo /var/lib/hitstor/repo --password "REPO_PASSWORD"

For production systems, use a password file or environment variable instead of passing the password on the command line:

export HITSTOR_PASSWORD="REPO_PASSWORD"
hitstor init --repo /var/lib/hitstor/repo

docs.title: Start the Server
docs.text:
Start the HitStor server with gRPC and dashboard ports:

hitstor serve --repo /var/lib/hitstor/repo --port 8420 --dashboard-port 8421

The server opens two listeners:

Port Protocol Purpose 8420 gRPC (TLS) Agent communication -- backups, restores, scheduling 8421 HTTP Web dashboard and JSON API

The server runs in the foreground. Use systemd (see below) for production deployments.

docs.title: Repository Password
docs.text:
The server needs the repository password to decrypt and encrypt data. There are three ways to provide it:

  1. Environment variable (recommended for production):

    export HITSTOR_PASSWORD="REPO_PASSWORD"
hitstor serve --repo /var/lib/hitstor/repo

  2. Password file:

    hitstor serve --repo /var/lib/hitstor/repo --password-file /etc/hitstor/password.txt

    The file should contain the password on a single line with no trailing newline. Set permissions to 0600.

  3. Command-line flag (not recommended for production):

    hitstor serve --repo /var/lib/hitstor/repo --password "REPO_PASSWORD"

docs.title: Configuration File
docs.text:
The server reads configuration from /etc/hitstor/config.yaml when the --config flag is set. A typical server configuration:

# /etc/hitstor/config.yaml
repo: /var/lib/hitstor/repo

# TLS certificates (optional, auto-generated if omitted)
serve_tls_cert: /etc/hitstor/tls/server.crt
serve_tls_key: /etc/hitstor/tls/server.key

# Dashboard
serve_dashboard_password: "DASHBOARD_PASSWORD"

# Alerting
alert_webhook_url: "https://hooks.example.com/hitstor"
alert_stale_threshold: 25

Start the server with the config file:

hitstor serve --config /etc/hitstor/config.yaml

See Configuration for the full schema and precedence rules.

docs.title: Multi-Repository Configuration
docs.text: HitStor supports managing multiple repositories from a single server instance. This is useful for separating backups by team, environment, or retention policy.

docs.title: Defining Repositories
docs.text:
Add a repositories section to the config file:

# /etc/hitstor/config.yaml
repositories:
  - name: production
    type: local
    path: /var/lib/hitstor/prod-repo
    password_file: /etc/hitstor/prod-password

  - name: staging
    type: local
    path: /var/lib/hitstor/staging-repo
    password_file: /etc/hitstor/staging-password

  - name: offsite
    type: s3
    endpoint: s3.amazonaws.com
    bucket: company-backups
    region: us-east-1
    access_key_encrypted: <encrypted by server>
    secret_key_encrypted: <encrypted by server>
    password_file: /etc/hitstor/s3-repo-password

S3 access keys are stored encrypted (access_key_encrypted, secret_key_encrypted). Use the dashboard Storage page to create S3 repositories without editing ciphertext manually.

Each repository must have a unique name. The type field must be local or s3.

docs.title: Backward Compatibility
docs.text: If the repositories list is empty and a repo field is present, the server operates in single-repo legacy mode using the repo path and HITSTOR_PASSWORD environment variable.

docs.title: Assigning Agents to Repositories
docs.text: Each agent targets a specific repository. Set the target repository from the Agent Detail page in the dashboard, or the agent will use the first configured repository by default.

docs.title: Managing Repositories from the Dashboard
docs.text: Repositories can also be created and removed from the dashboard Storage page. See Dashboard for details.

docs.title: TLS Certificates
docs.text: All gRPC communication between server and agents is encrypted with TLS.

docs.title: Auto-Generated (Default)
docs.text:
If no --tls-cert / --tls-key flags are provided, the server automatically generates a self-signed certificate on first startup and saves it to:

  • <repo>/server.crt — certificate (distribute to agents)
  • <repo>/server.key — private key (keep on server only)

The certificate includes all of the server's IP addresses and hostname in its Subject Alternative Names (SANs), so agents can connect by IP or hostname. The certificate is reused across server restarts.

To distribute the certificate to agents:

scp /var/lib/hitstor/repo/server.crt agent-host:/etc/hitstor/server.crt

Then configure each agent to trust it:

# Agent config.yaml
agent_ca_cert: /etc/hitstor/server.crt

Or via CLI flag:

hitstor-agent --ca-cert /etc/hitstor/server.crt ping

docs.title: Custom Certificates (Production)
docs.text:
For production, provide your own certificates:

hitstor serve --repo /var/lib/hitstor/repo \
  --tls-cert /etc/hitstor/tls/server.crt \
  --tls-key /etc/hitstor/tls/server.key

Or via config file:

serve_tls_cert: /etc/hitstor/tls/server.crt
serve_tls_key: /etc/hitstor/tls/server.key

If you use a certificate signed by a public CA, agents do not need the --ca-cert flag.

docs.title: Systemd Service
docs.text: On Linux systems installed via deb or rpm packages, a systemd unit is provided.

docs.title: Enable and Start
docs.text:
sudo systemctl enable hitstor-server
sudo systemctl start hitstor-server

docs.title: Environment File
docs.text:
The systemd unit reads environment variables from /etc/hitstor/server.env. Configure the repository password and any other settings here:

# /etc/hitstor/server.env
# Repository passwords are managed via the dashboard.
# For legacy single-repo mode:
# HITSTOR_PASSWORD=REPO_PASSWORD
# HITSTOR_REPO=/var/lib/hitstor/repo

Set permissions so only root can read the file:

sudo chmod 0600 /etc/hitstor/server.env
sudo chown root:root /etc/hitstor/server.env

docs.title: Check Status
docs.text:
sudo systemctl status hitstor-server
sudo journalctl -u hitstor-server -f

docs.title: Firewall Rules
docs.text:
Open the gRPC and dashboard ports on the server. For firewalld:

sudo firewall-cmd --permanent --add-port=8420/tcp
sudo firewall-cmd --permanent --add-port=8421/tcp
sudo firewall-cmd --reload

For ufw (Ubuntu/Debian):

sudo apt install ufw
sudo ufw allow 22/tcp comment "SSH"
sudo ufw allow 8420/tcp comment "HitStor gRPC"
sudo ufw allow 8421/tcp comment "HitStor Dashboard"
sudo ufw enable

Warning

Always allow SSH (port 22) before running ufw enable, or you may lose remote access to the server.

Verify the rules:

sudo ufw status verbose

If the dashboard should only be accessible from a management network, restrict port 8421 accordingly:

sudo ufw allow from 10.0.0.0/24 to any port 8421 proto tcp

docs.title: Log Output
docs.text:
HitStor uses Go's slog package for structured logging. Log output is JSON by default when running as a systemd service, making it easy to parse with tools like jq:

sudo journalctl -u hitstor-server -o cat | jq .

Increase verbosity with the --verbose flag:

Flag Level Description (none) warn Warnings and errors only -v info Operational messages (backup started, agent connected) -vv debug Detailed internal state (chunk processing, pack writes)

docs.text:

  • Agent Management -- register agents to connect to this server
  • Dashboard -- access the web dashboard

docs.title: Server Settings
docs.text: The Settings page (/settings) centralizes server configuration that was previously split across environment variables, YAML files, and CLI commands. It follows the same patterns as enterprise backup consoles: grouped sections, masked secrets, test-before-save, and a restart banner when network or TLS changes require it.

docs.title: Access
docs.text: Open System → Settings in the dashboard sidebar, or use a deep link (/settings?tab=integrations).

docs.title: Sections
docs.text: Tab What you configure General Update checks, parallel workers, sync writes, minimum free disk reserve Security & TLS Dashboard password, TLS certificate upload, certificate status Network gRPC port, dashboard HTTPS port, advertise address for agents Integrations Gemini API key (Sentinel) Notifications Alert webhook, stale-agent threshold

docs.title: Integrations
docs.text:
Configure integrations from Settings → Integrations:

  1. Gemini API key — encrypted at rest in config.yaml; used by Ransomware Sentinel when HITSTOR_SENTINEL_API_KEY is not set
  2. Gemini model — defaults to gemini-1.5-pro (or Sentinel default when unset)

Gemini is the only integration. SaaS and cloud-provider integrations were removed in v2.0.0 along with the workloads they served.

Use Test Gemini before saving. If you already have a value in an environment variable, click Import from environment to migrate it into encrypted YAML.

docs.title: TLS certificates
docs.text:
Upload a PEM certificate and private key from Security & TLS. Files are stored under /etc/hitstor/tls/ and paths are written to serve_tls_cert and serve_tls_key in the config file.

Restart required after upload — TLS is loaded at server startup.

The status card shows source (custom, repository auto-generated, or self-signed), subject, issuer, expiry, and SANs.

docs.title: Notifications
docs.text: alert_stale_threshold (default 25 hours) controls when agents are marked stale for alerting. Configure from Settings → Notifications.

docs.title: API
docs.text: See Dashboard HTTP API — Settings.
