The image is cached on the server rather than fetched from the host on demand. A design that rebuilt the ISO at download time would need the source host online and spend several minutes doing it, which breaks the feature in the one scenario it exists for.

docs.title: Capturing what a bare-metal restore needs
docs.text:
File contents alone do not describe a bootable machine. Add --bare-metal to a backup to capture the rest:

hitstor backup /etc /home /var --bare-metal

That records two things beyond the usual file tree:

  • Extended attributes — on Linux, SELinux contexts, file capabilities and POSIX ACLs are all xattrs, so one mechanism covers all three. Without them an SELinux system restores to an unlabeled filesystem whose services refuse to start.
  • The system profile — partition table, filesystem UUIDs and labels, LVM, software RAID, /etc/fstab, and bootloader state. Stored as an encrypted blob referenced from the snapshot, so the backup describes the machine's shape and not only its contents. The layout can be reconstructed even if the rescue media is lost.

Capture is best-effort throughout. A missing tool leaves that section empty and records a warning rather than failing the backup.

docs.title: Checking a host can build media
docs.text:
Run this on the protected host:

sudo hitstor-agent bmr check

It reports everything standing between that host and a bootable image at once — ReaR and its version, supporting tools, privileges — rather than stopping at the first problem, and exits non-zero when the host is not ready, so it can gate a provisioning script.

The same readiness appears per-host under Disaster Recovery → Bare Metal in the dashboard.

docs.title: Building the media
docs.text:
From the dashboard, under Disaster Recovery → Bare Metal, press Build media on a host. The server asks that host's agent to run ReaR and streams the resulting ISO back, showing the build as it happens. When it finishes, the image is cached on the server and Download appears.

Or on the host itself:

sudo hitstor-agent bmr build-media --server backup.example.com:8420

Useful flags:

Flag Purpose --migration-mode Allow recovery onto dissimilar hardware or a VM (P2V). ReaR remaps devices and regenerates the initramfs with the drivers the new hardware needs. --copy PATH Embed an extra file in the rescue image — a corporate CA bundle, say, without which the agent cannot verify the server. --agent NAME Registered agent name to prefill at the rescue prompt, when it differs from the hostname. --force Build despite readiness blockers.

rear mkrescue reads every disk on the machine and takes several minutes, so run it at a time when the extra load is acceptable.

Store the ISO somewhere that survives losing the host it came from.

docs.title: What is not on the media
docs.text:
No credentials. The recovery token, and where needed the repository password, are typed in at recovery time.

This is deliberate. Removable media that carried a working key would be a repository-compromise vector, and an ISO that still works a year after it was built, sitting on a shelf, is exactly the risk a long-lived credential creates. The cost is that unattended recovery is not possible unless you opt into it.

docs.title: Recovering a machine
docs.text:
1. Download that host's ISO from the Bare Metal tab and boot the replacement hardware from it.
  2. Back in the dashboard, press Issue token for the host. The token appears once — copy it. It works a single time, only for that host, and expires after 24 hours by default. If it leaks before use, Revoke it.
  3. At the rescue console, confirm the server address and agent name, then type the token. ReaR recreates the disk layout, mounts the new root at /mnt/local, and the recovery agent announces itself to the server.
  4. Return to Guided recovery and start the restore with the announced host as the target. Nothing starts on its own: a bare-metal restore is confirmed by an operator, like any other.
  5. When the restore reaches a terminal state the recovery agent exits, ReaR installs the bootloader, and the machine can be rebooted into the restored system.

docs.title: How the rescue host is reached
docs.text:
Every other restore is server-initiated: the server already knows an agent's address and dials in. A machine that just booted off rescue media has whatever address DHCP handed it, which nobody has told the server about.

So the rescue system calls home — presenting its recovery token and current address — and the server then dials back over the ordinary restore path, unchanged. The rescue system generates its own listener token for that dial-back; the original agent's token is never disclosed and stays valid for when the restored OS boots.

The server must be able to reach the rescue host

The dial-back needs a direct route to the address the rescue host announces. That holds for the same-LAN and P2V cases this release supports. A rescue host behind aggressive NAT across a WAN is not yet supported; the restore fails at start with the address it tried, rather than hanging.

docs.title: API
docs.text:
Method Path Description GET /api/bmr/hosts Per-host readiness and cached media POST /api/bmr/media/{agent}/build Start a build; returns an operation id GET /api/operations/{id}/events Build progress (SSE) GET /api/bmr/media/{agent}/download Download the cached ISO DELETE /api/bmr/media/{agent} Discard the cached ISO POST /api/bmr/prepare/{agent} Mint a recovery token (returned once) GET /api/bmr/tokens List outstanding tokens DELETE /api/bmr/tokens/{id} Revoke an unused token 
# Issue a token with a tighter window than the 24h default.
curl -sS -X POST "$SERVER/api/bmr/prepare/web-01" \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"ttl_hours": 2}'

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
bmr check reports blockers. Install what it names. On most distributions that is rear plus an ISO writer (xorriso or genisoimage). The command must run as root: ReaR reads raw block devices.

The build fails with a ReaR error. The message carries ReaR's own diagnosis. A previously cached image is left untouched — a rebuild that fails does not cost you the media you already had.

The rescue host announces but the restore will not start. The server could not reach the address it announced. Check routing and firewalls between the two, and that the port the rescue agent listens on (8422 by default) is open.

The token is rejected. Tokens are single-use, expire, and are bound to one host. Issue a fresh one; the error says which of the three applied.

docs.title: Related
docs.text:
• Disaster recovery — guided restore onto a booting host
  • Restore files — single-snapshot granular restore
  • Agents — install and register an agent

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text: HitStor can be configured through CLI flags, environment variables, and a YAML configuration file. This page explains how these sources interact, how to manage the config file, and how to use the interactive setup wizard.

docs.title: Config File Location
docs.text:
The default configuration file is located at:

~/.config/hitstor/config.yaml

HitStor creates this directory automatically the first time you run hitstor config init. You can also create the file manually.

docs.title: Precedence
docs.text:
When the same setting is specified in multiple places, HitStor applies the following precedence (highest to lowest):

  1. CLI flags -- always win.
  2. Environment variables -- override the config file.
  3. Config file -- provides persistent defaults.
  4. Built-in defaults -- used when nothing else is specified.

For example, if the config file sets repo: /backups/local but you pass --repo /backups/remote on the command line, the CLI flag takes effect.

docs.title: Environment Variables
docs.text:
The following environment variables are recognized:

Variable Purpose Example HITSTOR_REPO Default repository location export HITSTOR_REPO=/path/to/repo HITSTOR_PASSWORD Repository password export HITSTOR_PASSWORD=secret HITSTOR_PASSWORD_FILE Path to a file containing the password export HITSTOR_PASSWORD_FILE=/etc/hitstor/password.txt

When both HITSTOR_PASSWORD and HITSTOR_PASSWORD_FILE are set, HITSTOR_PASSWORD takes precedence.

Warning

Avoid setting HITSTOR_PASSWORD in shell profiles or scripts stored in version control. Use HITSTOR_PASSWORD_FILE with strict file permissions (e.g., chmod 600) for better security.

docs.title: Config Commands
docs.text: HitStor provides a set of subcommands for managing the configuration file without editing YAML by hand.

docs.title: config show
docs.text:
Display the current configuration:

hitstor config show
repo: /backups/local
password: ********
backup:
  exclude:
    - "*.tmp"
    - "node_modules"
  parallel: 4

Sensitive values such as passwords are masked in the output.

docs.title: config set
docs.text:
Set a single configuration key:

hitstor config set repo /backups/local
hitstor config set backup.parallel 4

Dot notation is used for nested keys.

docs.title: config unset
docs.text:
Remove a configuration key:

hitstor config unset backup.parallel

docs.title: config add
docs.text:
Append a value to a list-type key:

hitstor config add backup.exclude "*.log"
hitstor config add backup.exclude ".cache"

docs.title: config remove
docs.text:
Remove a value from a list-type key:

hitstor config remove backup.exclude "*.log"

docs.title: config init
docs.text: Launch the interactive setup wizard (see below).

docs.title: config edit
docs.text:
Open the config file in your default editor ($EDITOR or vi):

hitstor config edit

docs.title: config path
docs.text:
Print the absolute path to the config file:

hitstor config path
/home/user/.config/hitstor/config.yaml

docs.title: Interactive Setup Wizard
docs.text:
The config init command walks you through the essential settings interactively:

hitstor config init
Welcome to HitStor configuration.

Repository path []: /backups/local
Password []: ********
Default number of parallel workers (0 = auto) [0]: 4

Exclude patterns (one per line, empty line to finish):
> *.tmp
> node_modules
>

Configuration saved to /home/user/.config/hitstor/config.yaml

The wizard creates the config directory and file if they do not exist. If a config file already exists, the wizard pre-fills current values so you can update them selectively.

docs.title: Local Repository
docs.text:
A minimal config for backing up to a local disk:

repo: /mnt/external/hitstor-repo
password_file: /etc/hitstor/password.txt

backup:
  exclude:
    - "*.tmp"
    - ".cache"
    - "node_modules"
  parallel: 4

docs.title: S3 Repository
docs.text:
Backing up to an S3-compatible bucket:

repo: s3:s3.amazonaws.com/my-bucket/hitstor-repo
password_file: /etc/hitstor/password.txt

backup:
  exclude:
    - "*.tmp"
    - ".cache"
  parallel: 8

AWS credentials are configured through the standard environment variables (AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID, AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY) or the shared credentials file.

docs.title: Remote Agent Setup
docs.text:
When HitStor communicates with a remote agent for server-side processing:

repo: agent:user@backupserver:/data/hitstor-repo
password_file: /etc/hitstor/password.txt

backup:
  exclude:
    - "*.tmp"
  parallel: 4
  host: webserver-01

alerting:
  alert_notifier_plugins:
    - slack-notifier

docs.title: Sensitive Values
docs.text:
HitStor takes care not to expose sensitive configuration values:

  • config show masks passwords and tokens with ********.
  • The config file itself is not encrypted. Protect it with appropriate file-system permissions (chmod 600 ~/.config/hitstor/config.yaml).
  • Prefer password_file over storing the password directly in the config file. The file referenced by password_file should also have strict permissions.

Tip

You can combine the config file with environment variables for a layered approach: store non-sensitive defaults in the config file and inject passwords through HITSTOR_PASSWORD_FILE at runtime.

docs.title: Disaster recovery (guided full-system restore)
docs.text: HitStor protects filesystems, not raw disks. Disaster recovery means rebuilding a host from its file backups onto new or repaired hardware with a guided dashboard wizard.

docs.title: What this is (and is not)
docs.text:
Is Is not Full restore of all backup jobs for a system Block-level disk imaging Sequential restore of each job’s latest snapshot Automatic OS reinstall / bootloader repair Staging root or original-path modes Hypervisor VM import

After the OS and HitStor agent are installed on the recovery host, the wizard restores application and data paths from the repository.

For a machine with a blank disk — no OS to install an agent onto, no partition table to restore into — see Bare-metal restore, which recreates the disk layout and bootloader first and then hands the data restore back to this wizard.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
1. Recovery host has a compatible OS (Windows or Linux).
  2. HitStor agent installed and registered with the backup server.
  3. Enough free disk for the data (or a large staging volume).
  4. Source system’s backup jobs have completed at least once (snapshots present).

Optional but recommended: jobs with restore verification green (see Backups page).

docs.title: Dashboard wizard
docs.text:
Open Disaster Recovery in the sidebar (/disaster).

  1. Select system — protected agent (source) with jobs/snapshots.
  2. Review plan — each job’s latest snapshot, paths, size, last verify status.
  3. Target agent — usually the new host; can be the same agent after rebuild.
  4. Mode
  5. Staging root (default): restore under e.g. /recover/hostname/job-name for review, then cut over.
  6. Original paths: write to live paths (stop services that lock files first).
  7. Start full-system recovery — restores run one job after another on the target agent.

Progress appears on the same page (and under Restores for individual sessions).

docs.title: API (operators / automation)
docs.text:
Method Path Description GET /api/disaster/plans Summary of systems and readiness GET /api/disaster/plans/{agent} Full plan + checklist POST /api/disaster/recover Start recovery GET /api/disaster/recoveries List orchestrated recoveries GET /api/disaster/recoveries/{id} One recovery status

Example:

curl -sS -X POST "$SERVER/api/disaster/recover" \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{
    "source_agent": "web-01",
    "target_agent": "web-01-new",
    "mode": "staging",
    "staging_root": "/recover/web-01"
  }'

docs.title: After recovery
docs.text:
1. Validate application data under staging (or live paths).
  2. Cut over DNS/services as needed.
  3. Re-point or recreate backup jobs on the recovery agent.
  4. Optionally run hitstor verify-restore <snapshot> for an extra integrity check.

docs.title: Related
docs.text:
• Bare-metal restore — recovering a machine with a blank disk
  • Restore files — single-snapshot granular restore
  • Agents — install/register recovery host
  • Benchmarks — restore performance expectations

docs.title: Getting Started
docs.text: This tutorial walks you through the core HitStor workflow from start to finish. By the end you will have initialized a repository, created backups, listed snapshots, restored files, verified integrity, and applied a retention policy.

docs.title: Initialize a Repository
docs.text:
A repository is the directory where HitStor stores encrypted, deduplicated backup data. Before you can create any backups you must initialize one.

hitstor init --repo /path/to/repo --password "secret"
created hitstor repository at /path/to/repo

The --repo flag points to the target directory (it will be created if it does not exist). The --password flag supplies the encryption passphrase that protects all data in the repository.

Warning

Remember your password. Without it, the data in the repository is unrecoverable. Consider storing the password in a password manager or using HITSTOR_PASSWORD_FILE to read it from a file.

docs.title: Create Your First Backup
docs.text:
Back up a directory by passing its path as the final argument:

hitstor backup --repo /path/to/repo --password "secret" /data
snapshot abc12345 saved
  Files:        1,247 new,     0 changed,     0 unmodified
  Dirs:            38 new,     0 changed,     0 unmodified
  Data:       512.00 MiB added
  Processed:  1,247 files, 512.00 MiB in 0:08

HitStor splits every file into variable-length chunks, deduplicates them, compresses them, and encrypts the result before writing it to the repository.

docs.title: List Snapshots
docs.text:
Each backup produces a snapshot -- a point-in-time record of the files that were backed up. List all snapshots with:

hitstor snapshots --repo /path/to/repo --password "secret"
ID        Time                 Host        Tags    Paths
------------------------------------------------------------------------
abc12345  2026-02-22 10:00:05  myhost              /data

docs.title: Create a Second Backup (Incremental Behavior)
docs.text:
Run the same backup command again after making a few changes to /data:

hitstor backup --repo /path/to/repo --password "secret" /data
snapshot def67890 saved
  Files:           3 new,     5 changed, 1,239 unmodified
  Dirs:            0 new,     2 changed,    36 unmodified
  Data:        4.20 MiB added
  Processed:  1,247 files, 512.00 MiB in 0:01

Notice how much faster the second backup is. HitStor only stores the chunks that are new or modified; unchanged data is deduplicated automatically.

hitstor snapshots --repo /path/to/repo --password "secret"
ID        Time                 Host        Tags    Paths
------------------------------------------------------------------------
abc12345  2026-02-22 10:00:05  myhost              /data
def67890  2026-02-22 10:15:32  myhost              /data

docs.title: Restore from a Snapshot
docs.text:
To restore the contents of a snapshot to a target directory, pass the snapshot ID and the destination path:

hitstor restore --repo /path/to/repo --password "secret" abc12345 /restore/path
restoring snapshot abc12345 to /restore/path
  Files:  1,247 restored
  Dirs:      38 restored

You can use the full snapshot ID or a unique short prefix (the first 8 or more characters). You can also use the keyword latest to restore the most recent snapshot:

hitstor restore --repo /path/to/repo --password "secret" latest /restore/path

docs.title: Verify the Repository
docs.text:
The check command verifies the structural integrity of the repository. It reads every pack file, validates checksums, and confirms that all referenced data is present.

hitstor check --repo /path/to/repo --password "secret"
using temporary cache in /tmp/hitstor-check-123456
repository structure is ok
all pack files verified
no errors found

Run check periodically -- especially before and after migrating repository data -- to catch corruption early.

docs.title: Apply a Retention Policy
docs.text:
Over time the number of snapshots grows. The forget command removes snapshots that fall outside a retention policy, and the prune command reclaims the disk space used by data that is no longer referenced.

hitstor forget --repo /path/to/repo --password "secret" \
    --keep-last 7 \
    --keep-daily 30
Applying retention policy:
  keep the last 7 snapshots
  keep daily snapshots for 30 days

remove 0 snapshots

In this example both snapshots are recent enough to be retained. As your snapshot history grows, older snapshots that do not satisfy any policy rule will be removed.

docs.title: Reclaim Disk Space
docs.text:
After forget marks snapshots for removal, the underlying data chunks may still be present. Run prune to delete unreferenced data and repack partially-used pack files:

hitstor prune --repo /path/to/repo --password "secret"
counting files in repo
finding data still in use for 2 snapshots
[0:00] 100.00%  2 / 2 snapshots
searching used packs...
collecting packs for deletion and repacking
  no packs to delete or repack
done

When there is unreferenced data to clean up, prune reports exactly how much space was reclaimed.

docs.title: Next Steps
docs.text:
Now that you understand the basic workflow you can explore the rest of the User Guide:

  • Backup -- advanced backup options, exclude patterns, and parallel workers.
  • Restore -- selective restores, permissions, and verification.
  • Snapshots -- filtering, comparing, and inspecting snapshots.
  • Retention -- fine-grained retention strategies and automated pruning.
  • Configuration -- config file, environment variables, and the setup wizard.
  • Plugins -- extend HitStor with storage backends, notifiers, hooks, and scanners.

docs.title: Plugins
docs.text:
HitStor extends functionality through external plugin binaries using the HashiCorp go-plugin framework. Plugins communicate with HitStor over gRPC subprocesses, not stdin/stdout.

For plugin development details, see Plugin Development.

docs.title: Plugin Discovery
docs.text:
HitStor searches for plugin binaries in:

  1. plugin_dir config path (checked first)
  2. $PATH
plugin_dir: /usr/local/lib/hitstor/plugins

docs.title: Binary Naming Convention
docs.text: Plugin Type Pattern Example Storage backend hitstor-backend-NAME hitstor-backend-memory Notifier hitstor-notifier-NAME hitstor-notifier-slack Hook hitstor-hook-NAME hitstor-hook-log

docs.title: Built-in Plugin Binaries
docs.text:
The filesystem scanner (hitstor-scanner-builtin) is the core built-in plugin and is installed with the agent/server packages into the standard plugin directory. It provides Linux and Windows filesystem backup.

Other plugins (storage backend, notifier, hook) are optional and extend how backups are stored, alerted on, or triggered around.

Build all plugins:

make plugins
Binary Purpose Installed by default? hitstor-scanner-builtin Core filesystem scanner (Linux/Windows) Yes (core package) hitstor-backend-memory In-memory storage (testing) No hitstor-notifier-log Log notifier example No hitstor-hook-log Hook example No

docs.title: Storage Backend Plugins
docs.text:
hitstor init --repo plugin:memory --password "secret"
hitstor backup --repo plugin:memory --password "secret" /data

docs.title: Notifier Plugins
docs.text:
alert_notifier_plugins:
  - slack
plugin_dir: /usr/local/lib/hitstor/plugins

Also configure alert_webhook_url for the built-in webhook notifier. Multiple notifiers can run in parallel.

docs.title: Hook Plugins
docs.text:
hook_plugins:
  - log

Hooks fire at PreBackup and PostBackup. Pre-backup errors abort the backup; post-backup errors are logged only.

docs.title: Filesystem Scanner Plugins
docs.text:
Only one scanner plugin is active at a time:

fs_scanner_plugin: builtin   # default walker

Use builtin for the default walker, or the name of a custom filesystem scanner plugin you have installed.

docs.title: Installing Plugins
docs.text:
cp bin/hitstor-scanner-myfs /usr/local/lib/hitstor/plugins/
chmod +x /usr/local/lib/hitstor/plugins/hitstor-scanner-myfs

No restart is required — plugins are spawned on demand.

docs.title: See Also
docs.text: • Plugin Development

docs.title: Restore
docs.text: The hitstor restore command extracts files from a snapshot and writes them to a target directory. You can restore an entire snapshot or select individual files and directories.

docs.title: Basic Usage
docs.text:
hitstor restore --repo /path/to/repo --password "secret" SNAPSHOT_ID /target

This recreates the full directory tree captured in the specified snapshot under /target.

hitstor restore --repo /path/to/repo --password "secret" abc12345 /restore/path
restoring snapshot abc12345 to /restore/path
  Files:  1,247 restored
  Dirs:      38 restored

docs.title: Snapshot ID Resolution
docs.text: HitStor supports three ways to identify the snapshot you want to restore.

docs.title: Full ID
docs.text:
The complete hexadecimal snapshot identifier as shown by hitstor snapshots:

hitstor restore --repo /path/to/repo --password "secret" \
    abc12345def67890abc12345def67890abc12345def67890abc12345def67890 /target

docs.title: Short Prefix
docs.text:
Any unique prefix of 8 or more characters:

hitstor restore --repo /path/to/repo --password "secret" abc12345 /target

If the prefix matches more than one snapshot, HitStor reports an error and asks you to provide a longer prefix.

docs.title: The latest Keyword
docs.text:
The word latest resolves to the most recent snapshot in the repository:

hitstor restore --repo /path/to/repo --password "secret" latest /target

When the repository contains snapshots from multiple hosts or paths, latest picks the single most recent snapshot regardless of host or path. Combine with --host or --path in the snapshots command first to identify the exact snapshot you need.

docs.title: Selective Restore with --include
docs.text:
To restore only a subset of files, use --include with a glob pattern:

hitstor restore --repo /path/to/repo --password "secret" \
    --include "*.pdf" \
    abc12345 /target

Multiple --include flags can be combined. A file is restored if it matches any of the patterns:

hitstor restore --repo /path/to/repo --password "secret" \
    --include "documents/**" \
    --include "photos/2026/**" \
    abc12345 /target

Only the matching files and their parent directories are created in the target.

docs.title: Restoring to a Different Location
docs.text:
The target path does not need to match the original backup path. You can restore to any writable directory:

hitstor restore --repo /path/to/repo --password "secret" \
    abc12345 /tmp/recovery

The directory structure from the snapshot is recreated under the target. For example, if the snapshot contains /data/reports/q1.pdf, the restored file appears at /tmp/recovery/data/reports/q1.pdf.

docs.title: File Ownership and Permissions
docs.text:
HitStor records POSIX file metadata -- ownership (UID/GID), permissions, and timestamps -- in every snapshot.

During restore:

  • Permissions are applied as recorded. If the current user does not have permission to set a given mode, the file is created with the user's default umask and a warning is printed.
  • Ownership is restored only when the restore runs as root. Non-root restores set the owner to the current user.
  • Timestamps (modification time and access time) are restored for both files and directories.

Note

On filesystems that do not support POSIX permissions (for example, FAT32), ownership and permission metadata are silently ignored.

docs.title: Progress Display
docs.text:
Restore operations display live progress showing:

  • Number of files restored so far
  • Amount of data written
  • Elapsed time

Example output during a restore:

[0:05] 73.20%  912 / 1,247 files  375.00 MiB / 512.00 MiB

When output is redirected to a file or pipe, HitStor prints only the final summary.

docs.title: Verifying Restored Data
docs.text: After a restore it is good practice to verify that the output matches the snapshot contents. Two approaches are available:

docs.title: Compare File Counts
docs.text:
List the snapshot contents and compare against the restored tree:

hitstor ls --repo /path/to/repo --password "secret" abc12345 | wc -l
1247

find /restore/path -type f | wc -l
1247

docs.title: Use hitstor check
docs.text:
The check command verifies repository integrity at the storage level, which confirms that the data backing the snapshot is not corrupted:

hitstor check --repo /path/to/repo --password "secret"

docs.title: Checksum Verification
docs.text:
For critical restores, generate checksums of the original files (before or during backup) and compare them against the restored copies:

cd /restore/path && sha256sum -c /path/to/checksums.txt

Tip

If you suspect data corruption, run hitstor check first. If the repository passes all checks, the restore output is trustworthy.

docs.title: Retention
docs.text: As you take regular backups, the number of snapshots grows steadily. The hitstor forget command removes snapshots that no longer match a retention policy, and hitstor prune reclaims the disk space occupied by data that is no longer referenced by any remaining snapshot.

docs.title: Removing Individual Snapshots
docs.text:
You can remove specific snapshots by passing their IDs directly:

hitstor forget --repo /path/to/repo --password "secret" abc12345 def67890
removed snapshot abc12345
removed snapshot def67890

This is useful for one-off cleanup, but for routine maintenance a policy-based approach is more practical.

docs.title: Policy-Based Retention
docs.text: Instead of specifying individual IDs, define rules that describe which snapshots to keep. Everything that does not match any rule is removed.

docs.title: Available Policy Flags
docs.text: Flag Keeps --keep-last N The N most recent snapshots --keep-hourly N The most recent snapshot for each of the last N hours that have a snapshot --keep-daily N The most recent snapshot for each of the last N days that have a snapshot --keep-weekly N The most recent snapshot for each of the last N weeks that have a snapshot --keep-monthly N The most recent snapshot for each of the last N months that have a snapshot --keep-yearly N The most recent snapshot for each of the last N years that have a snapshot --keep-tag TAG Every snapshot that carries the specified tag

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
Keep the 7 most recent snapshots and one daily snapshot for the last 30 days:

hitstor forget --repo /path/to/repo --password "secret" \
    --keep-last 7 \
    --keep-daily 30

Keep one snapshot per month for one year, plus all snapshots tagged important:

hitstor forget --repo /path/to/repo --password "secret" \
    --keep-monthly 12 \
    --keep-tag important

docs.title: Union Semantics
docs.text:
Retention policies use union semantics: a snapshot is kept if it matches any of the active rules. Rules are not applied sequentially or exclusively; they are evaluated independently and their results are combined.

For example, with --keep-last 3 --keep-daily 7:

  • A snapshot is kept if it is one of the 3 most recent, or if it is the latest snapshot for one of the last 7 calendar days.
  • A snapshot that satisfies both rules is still kept (the rules do not cancel each other out).

docs.title: Host and Path Filtering
docs.text: By default, forget applies the retention policy across all snapshots in the repository, grouped by host and path. You can narrow the scope with filters:

docs.title: Filter by Host
docs.text:
hitstor forget --repo /path/to/repo --password "secret" \
    --host webserver \
    --keep-daily 14

Only snapshots recorded from webserver are evaluated. Snapshots from other hosts are untouched.

docs.title: Filter by Path
docs.text:
hitstor forget --repo /path/to/repo --password "secret" \
    --path /var/www \
    --keep-last 5

Only snapshots whose backup path is /var/www are evaluated.

Both flags can be combined to target a specific host-and-path combination.

docs.title: Dry Run
docs.text:
Before committing to a retention policy, preview its effect with --dry-run:

hitstor forget --repo /path/to/repo --password "secret" \
    --keep-last 7 \
    --keep-daily 30 \
    --dry-run

The command prints exactly which snapshots would be kept and which would be removed, without actually deleting anything. Always run --dry-run first when tuning a new policy.

Example dry-run output:

Applying retention policy to 15 snapshots:
  keep 7 snapshots:
    abc12345  bcd23456  cde34567  def45678  efg56789  fgh67890  ghi78901
  remove 8 snapshots:
    hij89012  ijk90123  jkl01234  klm12345  lmn23456  mno34567  nop45678  opq56789

Dry run -- no snapshots removed.

docs.title: Automatic Prune
docs.text:
You can combine forget and prune into a single step by adding the --prune flag:

hitstor forget --repo /path/to/repo --password "secret" \
    --keep-last 7 \
    --keep-daily 30 \
    --prune

This removes the snapshots that fall outside the retention policy and immediately reclaims the disk space for any unreferenced data. It is equivalent to running forget followed by prune as separate commands.

docs.title: Separate Prune Step
docs.text:
If you prefer to decouple snapshot removal from space reclamation, run prune as a standalone command:

hitstor prune --repo /path/to/repo --password "secret"

prune scans the repository for data chunks that are no longer referenced by any snapshot and deletes them. It also repacks partially-used pack files to reduce fragmentation.

docs.title: Limiting Repack Size
docs.text:
For very large repositories, repacking can involve significant I/O. Use --max-repack-size to cap the amount of data repacked in a single run:

hitstor prune --repo /path/to/repo --password "secret" \
    --max-repack-size 5G

This processes up to 5 GiB of pack data per invocation. Run prune again later to continue where it left off. This approach is useful for spreading the I/O cost over multiple maintenance windows.

docs.title: Development Workstation
docs.text:
Keep recent history for quick rollbacks, but do not accumulate months of snapshots:

hitstor forget --repo /path/to/repo --password "secret" \
    --keep-last 3 \
    --keep-daily 7 \
    --keep-weekly 4 \
    --prune
  • Always have the last 3 snapshots available.
  • One snapshot per day for the past week.
  • One snapshot per week for the past month.

docs.title: Production Server
docs.text:
Maintain a longer history with monthly granularity for auditing:

hitstor forget --repo /path/to/repo --password "secret" \
    --host production-db \
    --keep-last 7 \
    --keep-daily 30 \
    --keep-weekly 12 \
    --keep-monthly 24 \
    --prune
  • Last 7 snapshots for immediate recovery.
  • Daily snapshots for the past month.
  • Weekly snapshots for the past 3 months.
  • Monthly snapshots for the past 2 years.

docs.title: Compliance / Long-Term Archival
docs.text:
Regulations may require retaining data for several years:

hitstor forget --repo /path/to/repo --password "secret" \
    --keep-daily 90 \
    --keep-monthly 36 \
    --keep-yearly 7 \
    --keep-tag compliance \
    --prune
  • Daily snapshots for the past 90 days.
  • Monthly snapshots for the past 3 years.
  • Yearly snapshots for the past 7 years.
  • Any snapshot tagged compliance is kept indefinitely.

Tip

Schedule forget --prune as a cron job or systemd timer so that retention policies are applied automatically. See the Admin Guide for automation recipes.

docs.title: Snapshots
docs.text: Every time you run hitstor backup, a new snapshot is created. A snapshot is a metadata record that points to the deduplicated chunks making up your files at a specific point in time. This page covers how to list, filter, compare, and inspect snapshots.

docs.title: List All Snapshots
docs.text:
hitstor snapshots --repo /path/to/repo --password "secret"
ID        Time                 Host        Tags        Paths
----------------------------------------------------------------------------
abc12345  2026-02-20 08:00:12  webserver   daily       /var/www
bcd23456  2026-02-21 08:00:09  webserver   daily       /var/www
cde34567  2026-02-22 08:00:11  webserver   daily       /var/www
def45678  2026-02-22 10:30:00  laptop      manual      /home/user

The hitstor ls alias works identically:

hitstor ls --repo /path/to/repo --password "secret"

docs.title: By Host
docs.text:
Show only snapshots recorded from a specific host:

hitstor snapshots --repo /path/to/repo --password "secret" --host webserver
ID        Time                 Host        Tags        Paths
----------------------------------------------------------------------------
abc12345  2026-02-20 08:00:12  webserver   daily       /var/www
bcd23456  2026-02-21 08:00:09  webserver   daily       /var/www
cde34567  2026-02-22 08:00:11  webserver   daily       /var/www

docs.title: By Path
docs.text:
Show only snapshots that include a specific backup path:

hitstor snapshots --repo /path/to/repo --password "secret" --path /home/user
ID        Time                 Host        Tags        Paths
----------------------------------------------------------------------------
def45678  2026-02-22 10:30:00  laptop      manual      /home/user

docs.title: Combining Filters
docs.text: --host and --path can be used together. A snapshot must match both filters to appear.

docs.title: JSON Output
docs.text:
For scripting and integration with other tools, use --json to produce machine-readable output:

hitstor snapshots --repo /path/to/repo --password "secret" --json

The output is a JSON array of snapshot objects:

[
  {
    "id": "abc12345...",
    "time": "2026-02-20T08:00:12Z",
    "host": "webserver",
    "tags": ["daily"],
    "paths": ["/var/www"]
  },
  ...
]

This is useful for piping into jq or other JSON processors:

hitstor snapshots --repo /path/to/repo --password "secret" --json \
    | jq '.[].id'

docs.title: Understanding Snapshot IDs
docs.text: Each snapshot is identified by a hexadecimal string derived from a cryptographic hash of its contents. In the default table output, IDs are shown as a short prefix (typically 8 characters).

docs.title: Short Prefix Matching
docs.text:
Whenever a command accepts a snapshot ID, you can provide a short prefix instead of the full hex string. The prefix must be long enough to uniquely identify one snapshot in the repository. If the prefix is ambiguous, HitStor prints an error listing the matching snapshots so you can provide a longer prefix.

hitstor snapshots --repo /path/to/repo --password "secret"
ID        ...
--------  ...
abc12345  ...
abc12399  ...

hitstor restore --repo /path/to/repo --password "secret" abc123 /target
Fatal: prefix "abc123" matches multiple snapshots: abc12345, abc12399

hitstor restore --repo /path/to/repo --password "secret" abc12345 /target
restoring snapshot abc12345 ...

docs.title: The latest Keyword
docs.text: The keyword latest can be used in place of a snapshot ID. It resolves to the most recent snapshot in the repository (by timestamp).

docs.title: Comparing Snapshots
docs.text:
The hitstor diff command shows what changed between two snapshots:

hitstor diff --repo /path/to/repo --password "secret" abc12345 bcd23456

The output lists files that were added, removed, or modified:

+    /var/www/blog/new-post.html
-    /var/www/old-page.html
M    /var/www/index.html
M    /var/www/css/style.css
Prefix Meaning + File added in the second snapshot - File removed in the second snapshot M File modified between the two snapshots

This is helpful for auditing what changed between backups or verifying that an expected set of changes was captured.

docs.title: Disk Usage
docs.text:
The hitstor du command reports how much repository space is consumed by one or more snapshots:

hitstor du --repo /path/to/repo --password "secret"
Snapshot    Size
---------------------
abc12345    512.00 MiB
bcd23456      4.20 MiB
cde34567      3.80 MiB
def45678    128.00 MiB
---------------------
Total:      648.00 MiB

Because of deduplication, the per-snapshot sizes reflect only the unique data each snapshot contributes. The total may be much smaller than the sum of the original file sizes across all snapshots.

Note

hitstor du reads the repository index and does not download or decrypt the actual data, so it is fast even for large repositories.

docs.title: HitStor
docs.text: Herramienta de respaldo cifrada y con deduplicación, escrita en Go.

docs.title: Resumen
docs.text: HitStor ofrece respaldos seguros y eficientes con cifrado del lado del cliente, deduplicación definida por contenido y compresión. Admite backends de almacenamiento locales y compatibles con S3, agentes de respaldo remotos sobre gRPC/TLS, un dashboard web y una arquitectura de plugins extensible.

docs.title: Características principales
docs.text:
• Cifrado del lado del cliente: AES-256-GCM con derivación de claves scrypt
  • Deduplicación definida por contenido: división en fragmentos (chunks) con FastCDC (256 KiB–4 MiB)
  • Compresión: compresión Zstd por fragmento antes del cifrado
  • Servidor de respaldo remoto: servidor gRPC con TLS y autenticación por clave de API
  • Dashboard web: tareas de respaldo, agentes, almacenamiento, restauración y flujos de DR
  • Restauración bare-metal: medios de recuperación basados en ReaR para hosts Linux
  • Arquitectura de plugins: almacenamiento, notificadores, hooks y escáneres de sistemas de archivos (go-plugin gRPC)
  • E/S en paralelo: pools de workers para respaldos y restauraciones más rápidos
  • Un único binario estático: despliegue sin dependencias con CGO_ENABLED=0

docs.title: Inicio rápido
docs.text:
# Instalar (deb para Linux)
sudo dpkg -i hitstor_0.1.0_amd64.deb

# Inicializar un repositorio
hitstor init --repo /var/lib/hitstor/repo --password "secret"

# Crear un respaldo
hitstor backup --repo /var/lib/hitstor/repo --password "secret" /data

# Listar instantáneas
hitstor snapshots --repo /var/lib/hitstor/repo --password "secret"

# Restaurar
hitstor restore --repo /var/lib/hitstor/repo --password "secret" latest /restore
